Activation Functions: Understanding tanh

Tanh edition · A continuation of the representation-space exercise.

Learning objective

Demonstrate how a nonlinear activation function transforms a straight-line pattern of pre-activation values into a nonlinear pattern of activation values.

The weighted sum + bias is an affine operation. The activation function introduces nonlinearity.

How did the network reshape this representation space?

In the previous exercise, the representation space was reshaped, changing the relative positions of observations so that a straight decision boundary could separate the classes.

What made this reshaping possible? Nonlinear activation functions. They allow a neural network to go beyond straight-line transformations, bending and folding the representation space, as illustrated in this example.

1. Why do we need activation functions?

Linear (or affine) transformations can stretch, compress, rotate, and shear a representation space, but they cannot bend or fold it. Nonlinear activation functions enable neural networks to learn transformations that can bend and fold a representation space, making complex patterns easier to model and classes easier to separate.

Think of the representation space as a flexible sheet, with observations resting on it. When the sheet is reshaped, the observations move with it. Their new coordinates—and potentially their distances and relationships to other observations—change. The observations themselves have not changed; their representations have.

An affine transformation stretches, compresses, rotates, or shears the sheet without bending it. A nonlinear transformation can deform different regions differently, allowing the sheet to bend or fold. This is an analogy: real neural networks map numerical representations and may also change their dimensionality; they do not literally move a physical surface.

What will you discover?

In this exercise, you will see how a nonlinear activation function can transform a straight-line sequence of pre-activation values into a nonlinear pattern of outputs. Activation functions break proportionality. With a nonlinear activation function, equal changes in pre-activation values need not produce equal changes in activation values. This allows a straight-line input pattern to become a nonlinear output pattern. By adjusting the weight and bias, you will explore how different parts of that fixed function are encountered, changing the resulting activation pattern.

An affine transformation can stretch, shift, or reverse a straight line, but it cannot bend it. Composing affine layers is still affine.

Why do neural networks need nonlinear activation functions?
Without a nonlinear activation function, a neuron's output (a coordinate value) follows a straight-line relationship with its inputs, limiting its ability to model nonlinear patterns. For example, if a weight increases by 50%, its weighted contribution to the neuron's output also increases by 50%, assuming the input remains unchanged. Changing weights can alter the slope of this relationship, but cannot bend or fold it.

➜

2. An activation function: tanh

Find the pre-activation value on this chart’s x-axis; read the activation on its y-axis.

Never changes.

The tanh activation function smoothly transforms each pre-activation value into an output between −1 and 1. Negative inputs produce negative activations, tanh(0) = 0, and positive inputs produce positive activations. The output approaches −1 or 1 as the input moves farther from zero.

Gray points are reference values. Hover over an observation to trace its exact mapping.

➜

3. After: activation (node's output is now nonlinear)

Hover over an observation to see its activation value here.

By breaking proportionality in mapping pre-activation values to outputs, the neuron can now produce outputs (coordinate values) that follow a nonlinear pattern, even when its pre-activation values follow a straight line. This nonlinear transformation allows the network to model more complex relationships.

The bigger picture: Making classification easier

Same observations. New coordinates. The blue observations are surrounded by orange observations in the original representation. No single straight line can separate the two classes.

This is an illustration of a broader nonlinear transformation, not the exact operation performed by the single tanh neuron above.

Blue classOrange classDecision boundary (after)

Before: difficult to separate

The orange class surrounds the blue class. A straight boundary cannot separate them.

After: easier to separate

The gently warped grid illustrates how a nonlinear transformation can reshape the original coordinate space.

A nonlinear mapping changes the coordinates. Now one straight boundary separates the classes.

Think of the ground reshaping beneath the points. The observations remain the same, but their new positions relative to one another make classification easier.

Connection to neural networks: Training adjusts weights and biases, changing the pre-activation values sent to an activation function. The activation function itself usually remains fixed. This lab uses one input x, so m plays the role of a weight and b the bias. The concluding diagram illustrates the broader goal of learning a useful representation.
